en: Raced toward their elder;
Their two stirrups struck together.
Spurring in breathless haste,
They turned their horses' heads.
When they reached their elder,
They took their spears in hand;
The companions of fearsome bearing
Stood bristling and alert.
When the young men arrived and stood there,
The young lord Semetey,
As though his fierce mother Kanykey
Had given birth to a man indeed,
Smiled and beamed broadly,
His shovel-broad teeth gleaming,
His mail coat glittering upon him,
Your sovereign lord began to speak:
"Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
My matched pair of companions!
My cliff that even geese cannot circle,
My deeds before God must have been pure
For my God to give me you two.
My matched pair of companions,
Keep these words in mind:
Today I have seen a wonder.
Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
You are the morning stars above my head,
The costly beaver at my collar.
When I send you ahead, you are my open road;
When I place you behind, you are my countless host.
You are those I fondle and love,
Those who wear my bulletproof coat;
When an army comes covering the earth,
When force threatens my fly-sized soul,
You enter battle without a start!
Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
When you were infant children,
So that you would become stout-hearted heroes,
I had you fed slices of kazy;
So that you would be my own brothers,
I had both of you nurse
At Kanykey's breast!
You and your companion
Kicked each other like yearling colts
And nursed in rivalry at her breast.
My courser fit for a six-month ride,
The sustaining shadow of a toiling soul,
My dear kinsmen, let me cherish you!
Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
You possess a noble nature that commands the gaze;
You are vigorous legacies left to me
By the khans who departed long ago!
When I climb, you are my handhold;
When I descend, you are my support.
My two equal heroes,
Now I shall seek your counsel;
Listen to me, my champions!
Did you see what I saw?
Did you perceive what I perceived?
If you did not see what I saw,
If you did not perceive what I perceived,
You two foolish-born wretches—
In the valley of Great Opol,
Beside Great Urgench,
At the edge of the river water,
Among the birches and poplars,
Smoke rises into the sky.
Heed my words, young men:
White tents can be seen.
Bear-fur saddle cushions and white saddlecloths,
Their girths fastened tight,
Their breast straps firmly drawn,
The horses of fine young men can be seen.
A caravan has camped at the ford;
Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
Your needed road has appeared.
Smoke rises from the ridge;
Red-patterned saddles with bird-shaped pommels,
And maidens' horses can be seen.
Their girths are fastened,
And blankets drawn over them;
Saddles of maidens that would satisfy desire
If one went there can be seen.
At the sight, your elder cannot keep still;
His heart is deeply stirred.
Smoke billows upward;
Thirty daughters-in-law and thirty maidens,
Fortuitously placed upon your road,
Can be seen at play, young men.
Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
Whichever of you goes will find them there;
Together, you two have the strength of one man,
Cross the ford for me without delay;
These words I speak in counsel—
Bring me news without delay!
Go and engage them in conversation;
Ask about the condition
Of the falcon that went astray.
Ride out and reconnoiter the road;
Quickly bring back an answer
About the falcon that disappeared.
Will she agree to what you say?
Give my greetings to my brothers-in-law,
Ajybay and Tumenbay;
Will they give their sister?
Take six swift horses.
From the great khan, radiant as moonlight,
Who once received a palm-sized letter,
If he honors the spirits of old,
Tell him to abide by the ancient word;
Tell him to give an answer
About the falcon that disappeared.
Bring back a good answer,
Reconnoiter each stretch of the road.
That renowned Afghanistan—
Is Akun Khan a noble soul?
If Akun Khan has unexpectedly grown old,
Are all the numerous Afghans
People who would open fire?
If Akun Khan is a heroic khan,
Does he remember the pledged betrothal?
My matched pair of heroic companions,
You two companions, twinlike and equal as hairs,
Go safely and return unharmed.
Whichever one of you goes, go now;
Return quickly and do not keep me waiting.
If you set out mounted on a thoroughbred,
Keep the thoroughbred's mouth reined.
When she appears upon the open plain,
Give greetings and blessings
To Churok, daughter of Akun.
My Kanchoro, son of Chubak,
Like iron drawn and tempered,
I used to think you would become blue steel,
Burning everything in the direction you faced;
I used to think you would be fierce.
Your high brow was awe-inspiring,
And your radiance surpassed that of men.
To mount Kokborchuk,
Tire a horse and reconnoiter the land,
And travel far upon a journey;
To scout properly
The thirty daughters-in-law and thirty maidens,
And go obtain news
From beautiful Churok at her games—
How well suited are you for this, wrestler?"
Kanchoro stood stubbornly
And now answered in defiance.
Saying plainly, "I will not go,"
God now struck the poor man:
"I will not casually cross and scout the ford;
I have no skill with daughters-in-law.
While claiming to scout the crossing,
I will not fall into disgrace.
I will not scout your road along the cliffs;
I have no skill with maidens.
While claiming to scout the cliff road,
I will not fall into crime this way.
I have no words to find and say to a maiden;
I have no skill with women."
He said plainly, "I will not go."
God had taken hold of the young man;
The gray wolf born surpassing all men
Felt a little disappointment
In a young man like Kanchoro.
Turning away, he said this,
And your thoroughbred lord looked aside.
To twelve-year-old Kulchoro
He began to speak, poor man:
